output.query: post-cardiac arrest seizures status epilepticus treatment prognostication

results.key_finding: Multimodal neuroprognostication applies to patients who remain comatose 72 hours or more after return of circulation, once sedation is cleared; predictors include bilaterally absent N20, a highly malignant EEG after 24 hours, NSE above 60 mcg/L at 48 and/or 72 hours, status myoclonus within 72 hours and diffuse anoxic injury on CT or MRI.
results.title: European Resuscitation Council and European Society of Intensive Care Medicine guidelines 2021: post-resuscitation care

results.key_finding: Continuous EEG for at least 24 hours is recommended in comatose patients and when non-convulsive status epilepticus is suspected; status epilepticus is treated in stages with a benzodiazepine, then a second-line antiseizure drug, then an anaesthetic infusion if seizures continue.
results.title: Guidelines for the evaluation and management of status epilepticus

output.summary: Seizures and status epilepticus after cardiac arrest are treated with the same staged protocol as other status epilepticus, under continuous EEG [Brophy_2012]. Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective as second-line agents in ESETT [ESETT_2019]. ERC-ESICM multimodal prognostication is reserved for patients who remain comatose at 72 hours or later after return of circulation, and uses at least two concordant predictors [ERC_ESICM_2021]. Patients who regain consciousness fall outside that algorithm.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sodium 140, potassium 4.1, calcium 9.2, magnesium 1.9 and creatinine 0.9 normal; glucose 108; ALT 68 mildly raised; lactate 2.6 after the convulsion; troponin I 0.24 ng/mL and BNP 486 pg/mL raised five days after the arrest
action_criteria.label: Emergency laboratory work-up: glucose, CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, renal and hepatic function
action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of seizures and decide the ASM and its dose; potassium and magnesium also matter for arrhythmia risk five days after a VF arrest [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No acute intracranial abnormality: no hemorrhage, edema, mass effect or territorial infarct
action_criteria.label: Non-contrast head CT after stabilization
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes hemorrhage, mass or edema that would change management, and must precede any LP [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Continuous generalized spike-and-wave and polyspike-and-wave discharges at 2.5-3.5 Hz, bifrontal maximal, with time-locked bilateral arm myoclonus and a reactive slow background: NCSE by Salzburg criteria
action_criteria.label: Continuous video-EEG to confirm non-convulsive SE and monitor treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Persistent impaired consciousness after a convulsion, with staring spells beforehand, needs EEG confirmation of non-convulsive SE; continuous monitoring for at least 24 hours [Brophy_2012]; terminology [ACNS_2021].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus rhythm 64 with QTc 519 ms and broad low-amplitude T waves; no acute ST change, no paced complexes
action_criteria.label: 12-lead ECG: rhythm and QTc after a convulsion five days after a VF arrest
action_criteria.rationale: A convulsion in a patient with a recent VF arrest may be arrhythmic (convulsive syncope), and the QTc and conduction on amiodarone and metoprolol decide the second-line ASM [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral symmetric hippocampal restricted diffusion; no cortical, basal ganglia or thalamic injury
action_criteria.label: MRI brain with DWI for hypoxic-ischemic or peri-ictal injury
action_criteria.rationale: MRI is more sensitive than CT for hypoxic-ischemic injury and characterizes the substrate of new-onset SE after cardiac arrest [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Choose levetiracetam, which has no interaction; fosphenytoin loading risks bradycardia, AV block and hypotension and its level is raised by amiodarone, and lacosamide prolongs PR
action_criteria.label: Drug-interaction check: second-line ASM against amiodarone and metoprolol
action_criteria.rationale: She takes amiodarone and metoprolol: fosphenytoin and lacosamide interact with them, which decides the second-line ASM [ESETT_2019].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on post-anoxic SE and on the scope of coma prognostication
action_criteria.label: Literature: post-anoxic seizures and post-arrest prognostication
action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step [ERC_ESICM_2021].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not use fosphenytoin or phenytoin as the second-line drug: amiodarone inhibits its metabolism, and IV loading with amiodarone and metoprolol risks hypotension, bradycardia and AV block.

Do not limit or withdraw treatment on a presumed post-anoxic prognosis: she regained consciousness after the arrest, so coma prognostication criteria do not apply, and the current encephalopathy is treatable NCSE [ERC_ESICM_2021].
Do not add QT-prolonging drugs (for example haloperidol or a macrolide) with a QTc of 519 ms on amiodarone.
Do not induce anaesthetic coma before a benzodiazepine and a second-line ASM have been given [Brophy_2012].
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once), or IM midazolam 10 mg without IV access [Glauser_2016].

Load a second-line ASM: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg), and avoid fosphenytoin because on amiodarone and metoprolol its loading risks hypotension, bradycardia and AV block and amiodarone raises phenytoin levels [ESETT_2019].
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].
Interrogate the ICD and keep continuous cardiac telemetry to exclude a ventricular arrhythmia or device therapy at the time of the convulsion.

Admit to an ICU with airway monitoring; if seizures continue after the benzodiazepine and levetiracetam, treat as refractory SE with intubation and a midazolam or propofol infusion under cEEG [Brophy_2012].

avoided_actions.rationale: Amyloid PET has no role in HIE.
Carotid duplex not indicated — global ischemic injury, not embolic.

accepted: Post-anoxic non-convulsive status epilepticus with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest

differential.diagnosis: Convulsive syncope from a recurrent ventricular arrhythmia
differential.key_features: VF arrest 5 days ago with a new ICD makes an arrhythmic convulsion the first mimic; the ECG shows sinus rhythm and the EEG shows continuous electrographic seizures after the event, which syncope does not produce; ICD interrogation still required
Sodium, glucose, calcium, magnesium and creatinine are normal and ALT only mildly raised; the EEG shows discharges above 2.5 Hz with myoclonic correlate, not slow triphasic waves
Action myoclonus in an alert patient; here the myoclonus is time-locked to continuous generalized discharges with impaired consciousness
Typically 2 to 3 weeks after recovery with diffuse white matter change; at day 5 the MRI shows no white matter abnormality

key_clinical_evidence: A convulsion five days after a VF arrest needs an ECG and ICD interrogation to exclude an arrhythmic event before it is attributed to seizures
Staring spells and confusion beyond expectation since discharge, then a convulsion without return to baseline: continuous video-EEG shows NCSE with discharges above 2.5 Hz [Salzburg_NCSE_2015]
She woke and was extubated after the arrest, so coma neuroprognostication does not apply; the encephalopathy is treatable NCSE [ERC_ESICM_2021]
On amiodarone and metoprolol with a QTc of 519 ms, levetiracetam is the second-line ASM without a cardiac interaction [ESETT_2019]

patient.history_present_illness: A 55-year-old White female accountant was brought to the emergency department by her husband after a brief generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. The husband reports she convulsed for approximately 2 minutes and had not returned to her baseline level of alertness 35 minutes later. He was instructed to call 911. Critical history: the patient suffered a witnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest due to ventricular fibrillation 5 days ago. She was resuscitated after approximately 12 minutes of cardiac arrest (time from collapse to ROSC), intubated in the field, and was admitted to the cardiac ICU where she underwent targeted temperature management (TTM, 33°C for 24 hours) followed by controlled rewarming. She was extubated on day 3 and was discharged home on day 4 — somewhat prematurely in retrospect — with a newly implanted ICD. Since discharge she has been confused, more than expected, with prominent short-term memory impairment and episodes where she 'stares into space.' Her husband noted she had several brief 'staring spells' at home over the past 24 hours before today's convulsion. She takes aspirin, atorvastatin, amiodarone (started after the arrest), metoprolol and ramipril. Her husband reports the 'staring spells' were not recognized as seizures at discharge. No fever. No headache. No new cardiac symptoms. She was told post-cardiac arrest cognitive changes are 'normal' at discharge. Family history: mother with coronary artery disease. No epilepsy.
